name: Elixir
title: Elixir (1.20)

type.text: **Dynamic typing**: A term carries its type at run time, so `Map.get/2` on a list fails only when the call executes
**No declared types on functions**: A `def` head names patterns, not types, and the language has no type parameter or generic
**No sum types in the type system**: Alternatives are tagged tuples such as `{:ok, value}` and `{:error, reason}`, checked by pattern matching rather than by a type
**Dispatch is by run-time shape**: A protocol or a pattern chooses a clause from the value it receives, so no static check selects the branch
**`@spec` and Dialyzer give optional static analysis**: A success-typing pass detects a call whose arguments contradict the specification
**Gradual set-theoretic types are being added**: The work is in progress, so the language is dynamic today

construction.text: **Every value is immutable**: A term cannot be changed in place, so construction never aliases mutable state
**`defstruct` declares the record shape**: `%User{name: "Ada"}` builds a struct, and an unknown key is a compile-time error
**`@enforce_keys` validates at construction**: A struct with required keys cannot be built without them
**The pipe operator decouples data flow from nesting**: `data |> parse() |> validate()` reads left to right as a chain of transformations
**Processes hold state, not objects**: A `GenServer` keeps its state inside its own process, and a caller reaches it by message
**Mutable state lives in a named process or table**: `Agent`, `ETS`, and `:persistent_term` give shared state an explicit owner, so a reader can find it and an owner can delete it

memory.text: **BEAM collection is non-deterministic**: A process collects its heap when it grows, so the program does not choose the moment
**Each process has a private heap**: A collection pause is per-process and short, and there is no global stop-the-world collection
**No manual deallocation**: The VM reclaims memory, and a program never frees a term
**Large binaries live off-heap and are reference counted**: A binary above the heap-binary threshold is shared between processes rather than copied
**A large live set costs more to collect**: A long-lived `GenServer` that accumulates state pays a higher collection cost
**An ETS table lives outside the collector**: The table persists until its owner deletes it or dies

error.text: **Exceptions are unchecked**: `raise` and `throw` appear in no signature, so a caller cannot read the failure set from the type
**"Let it crash" plus supervision decouples recovery from business logic**: A `Supervisor` restarts a failed child, so the recovery path is not interleaved with the normal path
**Tagged tuples are the idiom for an expected failure**: `{:ok, value}` and `{:error, reason}` keep the failure inside the returned value
**`with` composes a chain of expected results**: Each `<-` clause fails through to the `else` branch without nesting
**Links and monitors make propagation explicit**: `spawn_link` and `Process.monitor` define which process observes a failure
**The tagged-tuple convention is not a type**: Nothing forces a caller to match the `:error` case, so the discipline is social

concurrency.text: **Processes are the unit of concurrency**: A BEAM process shares no memory and communicates by message, so a race between processes cannot occur
**The BEAM schedules preemptively**: A long computation is reduced and rescheduled, so one process cannot block a scheduler
**OTP gives structured, supervised concurrency**: `Task`, `Task.Supervisor`, `GenServer`, and `Supervisor` are library primitives over the process model
**Immutability removes locks from the model**: A message carries a value, and the receiver holds its own copy of the terms
**`Task.async` and `Task.await` pair a spawn with a result**: The caller collects results without a hand-written join
**A slow consumer accumulates messages**: An unbounded mailbox grows until the process is restarted

platform.text: **The BEAM is the only requirement**: Elixir code runs on any platform that runs an Erlang VM
**Erlang interop is direct**: Elixir calls Erlang modules and libraries without a binding layer
**Releases bundle the runtime**: `mix release` packages the BEAM, the application, and its dependencies into one deployable
**Nerves keeps the same model on embedded devices**: The build produces a firmware image, and the runtime model is unchanged
**The runtime is not a native binary**: A release carries the VM, so the artefact is larger than a compiled C program

performance.text: **The BEAM is a mature bytecode VM with a JIT**: BeamAsm, added in OTP 24, compiles hot code, so bytecode is not always interpreted
**Excellent for I/O-bound workloads**: Hundreds of thousands of processes can wait on I/O without one thread each
**Per-process collection avoids global pauses**: A collection affects one process, not the whole system
**Reduction-based scheduling keeps latency even**: No process starves another for long
**Weaker for CPU-bound computation**: The BEAM trails native-compiled languages on a tight numeric loop
**A NIF runs on a scheduler thread**: A long-running native function can block other processes on the same scheduler

ecosystem.text: **Hex.pm is a mature registry and `mix` is the build tool**: Dependency resolution, build tasks, and release packaging come from one toolchain
**Phoenix, Ecto, and LiveView cover web applications end to end**: Routing, database access, and server-rendered UI are provided by one family
**Erlang libraries are usable through interop**: The OTP libraries arrive with the runtime
**Livebook gives executable notebooks**: Interactive exploration and live documentation are part of the ecosystem
**The ecosystem is a monoculture around Phoenix and OTP**: One framework family dominates, so alternatives are few
**The library count is smaller than the JVM or npm**: Fewer general-purpose packages exist

evolution.text: **`mix.exs` pins an Elixir requirement**: A project states the version range it needs, and `mix` enforces it
**The BEAM is stable across decades**: Code written years ago continues to run
**Deprecations warn before removal**: The compiler emits a deprecation warning ahead of a change
**`mix format` settles style across the ecosystem**: One formatter removes style drift
**A hot upgrade needs a state migration callback**: `code_change/3` must convert old state to the new shape, so an upgrade is a design task

domain.text: **Excellent fit for real-time web**: Phoenix Channels push over WebSockets, and LiveView renders on the server
**Excellent fit for distributed, fault-tolerant systems**: OTP supervision and the distribution protocol cover process and node failure
**Nerves deploys to embedded devices**: The same runtime runs on a device image
**Back-pressure pipelines are a supported domain**: `GenStage` and `Broadway` build pipeline stages over processes
**Not aimed at CPU-bound numerics**: The BEAM is not designed for tight numerical loops

learning.text: **Ruby-like syntax lowers the barrier**: Developers from Ruby or another scripting language recognise the form
**The documentation culture is excellent**: HexDocs, guides, and doctests sit with the code
**The community is welcoming and growing**: Questions are answered and the ecosystem keeps expanding
**The surface is large**: The language, the OTP behaviours, macros, and the process model must all be learned
**Macros and `quote`/`unquote` are hard**: Metaprogramming is powerful and easy to misuse

syntax.text: **Ruby-inspired syntax is readable**: The `do`/`end` block form and the keyword style read naturally
**The pipe operator reads as data flow**: `|>` threads a value through a chain of calls
**Pattern matching replaces nested conditionals**: A multi-clause function is a case analysis
**Structs and maps have literal syntax**: `%User{name: "Ada"}` and `%{key: value}` build data directly
**Macros can hide the code they generate**: A DSL built with macros is opaque without the expansion
**The pipe passes the first argument**: An awkward argument order forces a wrapper function

testing.text: **ExUnit ships with the language**: `mix test` runs the suite with structured assertions and tagged tests
**Doctests run the examples in documentation**: An `iex>` example in `@doc` is executed as a test
**Property-based testing is available**: `StreamData` generates inputs from a property
**`mix test --trace` and coverage reporting are built in**: Test order and line coverage are visible without extra tooling
**Errors surface at run time**: Dynamic typing defers a type mistake to the executed path
**Testing concurrent code needs process-aware assertions**: A test must wait for a message or a process state, so timing is a factor

security.text: **Immutable data removes a class of shared-state faults**: No two processes share a mutable value
**Process isolation contains a fault**: A crashed process does not corrupt another process's heap
**Pattern matching makes an unexpected shape fail loudly**: A bad message raises a `FunctionClauseError` rather than corrupting state
**`String.to_atom/1` on untrusted input can exhaust the atom table**: Atoms are not collected, so untrusted conversion is a denial-of-service risk
**`Code.eval_string/1` executes arbitrary code**: Dynamic evaluation must be kept away from untrusted input
**A NIF and a `Port` reach unsafe code**: Native code can break the BEAM's safety guarantees

tradeoffs: **Dynamic typing is a deliberate trade**: It buys the flexibility of pattern matching and hot code loading at the cost of static checking
**Ruby-like syntax is a familiarity choice**: It lowers the barrier for developers from a scripting background
**LiveView keeps the UI state on the server**: This is a deliberate architectural choice that removes client JavaScript, not a language mechanism
**Nerves adds an embedded build layer**: The added layer is scope, not coupling
**Macros are a metaprogramming power**: A macro rewrites code at compile time, and that power carries the usual hygiene discipline
**The BEAM is a virtual machine, not an operating system**: The runtime boundary is scope, not a coupling defect
verdict: Elixir's design yields moderate language-imposed coupling. Immutable terms, the process model, and OTP supervision remove shared-memory races, turn failure into a supervision event, and keep state inside a process instead of in shared objects. Main strengths: the pipe operator and pattern matching decouple data flow and case analysis, the BEAM supports code loading without stopping the system, and the runtime is proven by decades of fault-tolerant operation. Main weaknesses: the language is dynamically typed, so a type fault surfaces at run time; exceptions are unchecked; collection is non-deterministic; and the ecosystem is a monoculture around Phoenix and OTP.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.
